query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor amount of Nb (~2 at.%) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA will promote the in situ formation of a fine, coherent Nb-rich secondary phase that impedes dislocation motion and improves both strength and creep resistance without sacrificing ductility or corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with insufficient strength and plasticity for industrial fastener applications
generation.intervention: Add approximately 2 atomic percent Nb during alloy synthesis to modify the composition
generation.conditions: The alloy is intended for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations (operating from ambient to moderately high temperatures, within the thermal stability limits of the alloy), long-term mechanical loading including room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments such as 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution
generation.structural_mediator: The Nb addition is expected to induce the precipitation of a coherent, Nb-rich secondary phase (similar to hard precipitates observed in related CoCrFeNi systems) finely dispersed within the FCC matrix
generation.mechanism: The Nb-rich precipitates will act as obstacles to dislocation movement (precipitation strengthening) and increase the elastic modulus locally, enhancing yield strength and creep resistance. Additionally, the Nb may contribute to improved corrosion resistance by forming stable Nb oxides at the surface under corrosive conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Nb-modified alloy should exhibit a measurable increase in yield strength and creep resistance while maintaining an acceptable level of ductility and corrosion resistance under the specified operating conditions
generation.baseline: The unmodified, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA
generation.boundary: Testing and operation should lie within the alloy’s thermal stability range (e.g., up to approximately 500°C or the maximum temperature before phase instability), with mechanical stresses comparable to those expected in industrial fastener applications and corrosion tests performed in environments such as a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Nb concentration, stability and coherence of the Nb-rich precipitates under long-term thermal cycling, and the detailed balance between improved strength and potential impact on ductility remain to be fully established through experimental optimization

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one set of the Nb-modified alloy (with ~2 at.% Nb added). Process both sets using identical thermomechanical treatments. Conduct tensile tests, room-temperature and elevated-temperature creep tests, corrosion tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, and accelerated thermal cycling to simulate extreme temperature fluctuations.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength (via tensile tests)
Creep rate and strain accumulation over time under controlled stress
Corrosion current density and pitting behavior (via electrochemical measurements)
Microstructural analysis (to confirm the presence, size, and distribution of Nb-rich precipitates using SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If statistical analysis shows that the Nb-modified alloy does not achieve at least a 10% improvement in yield strength and a measurable decrease in the creep rate (along with comparable or enhanced corrosion resistance) compared to the baseline alloy under the defined test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs) are composed of five or more elements at equal or nearly equal atomic ratios [,,,] HEAs tend to form a stable solid solution phase and have excellent mechanical properties and corrosion resistance, unlike the traditional alloys that are typically based on one or two principal elements. Therefore, HEAs have been heavily researched and attracted much attention from the academic community [,,]. The CoCrFeNi HEA system has become important, because of its excellent corrosion resistance, ductility, and thermal stability [,]. Surface engineering technologies, such as laser cladding and plasma spraying, can reduce the cost and increase the value of the HEAs for industrial applications []. However, the CoCrFeNi HEA system cannot meet the needs of high-strength parts due to its poor mechanical strength. It has been demonstrated that a hard secondary phase can be formed in the CoCrFeNi matrix by adding a small amount of Nb, Ti, or Mo, resulting in precipitation strengthening and improvement of the mechanical properties [].
